The best seller among shotguns in the United States is the 12 gauge pump gun with a 30-in. full-choke barrel. It is what the customers demand and, naturally, what the manufacturers supply. Such a gun is all right for deliberate pass-shooting at ducks at from 45 to 60 yd. And when fixed up with a special straight stock and ventilated rib, it is also a fine weapon for trapshooting. But pass-shooting at ducks and trap shooting account for perhaps 10 percent of the shotgun shells expended annually in the U. S. The humble cottontail, which is usually found in the brush at ranges of around 20 or 25 yd.—and which zigs and zags through the cover like a mad thing—is the No. 1 shotgun target in this country. Then there are the bobwhite and several sorts of Western quail, John Pheasant, woodcock, grouse of various kinds, and what not. Even decoyed ducks are generally taken at from 25 to 35 yd.—and for that shooting the hunter needs a full-choke gun with 30-in. barrels about as much as he needs a 10-ton truck to take Susie to the movies. Then by accident I made a discovery. I had got my brand-new bride a little 20 gauge Ithaca double with 26-in. barrels. Came a day when she wasn’t feeling right pert. The vagrant notion to try her gun came over me, so I laced on a recoil pad to lengthen the stock and went out to a brushy spot where I knew several large coveys of quail hung out. In fact, I’d been bombarding them with my Model 12 Winchester pump , and its full-choke 30-in. barrel had little effect on them. To my astonishment I found I could hit them quite neatly with the 20. I could get on them before they ducked behind a bush, follow them and cut them down when they tried to zig. I made one run of five straight, something I’d never done before in my life. The larger the gauge, of course, the more a barrel can be opened up. A modified 12 gauge puts as many shot pellets into a 30-in. circle at 40 yd. as a full-choke 20, and a 12 patterning 40 percent (about Skeet No. 1) throws 1 1/4 oz. of shot into as dense a pattern as a 20 gauge bored modified does with 1 oz. of shot. The common belief that a 20 gauge throws a smaller pattern than a 12 of the same boring is erroneous. The 20 simply throws a thinner pattern. We are a logical people—we think. We shake our heads in astonishment when told that the Hindus starve for protein while India is overrun by sacred cows. We chuckle at the quaint superstitions of the Navajo and Apache Indians, who refuse to eat wild turkey or trout. Yet we arm ourselves with smoothbores which, for 90 percent of our shooting, handicap us almost as much as if we went into the uplands with a 20-lb. weight tied to each foot. How come? Why this strange fixation on long-barreled, slow-handling, full-choke guns? Outdoor Li The average gunner is still sold on the ancient myth — a hangover from black-powder days—that the longer the barrel the “harder” a gun shoots. I get a stream of letters telling me about the marvelous ranging qualities of some fantastic old cannon or other, one with a 36 to 40-in. barrel, and described as the hardest-shooting gun in the community, capable of killing single ducks at 125 yd. Actually the standard 12 gauge load —3 3/4 drams of powder and 1 1/8 oz. of shot—reaches maximum velocity in a 30-in. barrel. The maximum loads— containing 3 1/4 drams of progressive burning powder and 1 1/4 oz. of shot— reach maximum velocity in a 32-in. barrel. But (and here’s the catch) velocity loss when a barrel is cut below maximum is only 6 ½ to 7 1/2 foot seconds for each inch amputated. The difference, then, between the velocity delivered by a clumsy, slow-handling 30-in. barrel and that of a fast-handling 26-in. barrel is only about 30 foot seconds—and there’s that much difference among shells from the same box fired in the same gun. A man could use a 30-in. barrel and a 26-in. barrel alternately until the cows came home and never discern any difference in killing power, penetration, or necessary lead. Another myth that needs exploding is the commonly held belief that a long barrel will pattern better than a short one. Within practical limits barrel length has nothing whatsoever to do with pattern. Pattern is determined by the degree of constriction (choke) at the muzzle and by the construction of the shot shell itself. I have patterned many a gun with a 26-in. barrel that gave patterns running 75 percent or better. There is nothing wrong with the long barrel for pass-shooting at waterfowl or for flight-shooting of doves. The long barrel tends to steady the swing and give more precise aim. However, the gun with the shorter barrel will do about as well if it is properly stocked and balanced. The momentum of the long-barreled, muzzle-heavy gun deters a man from slowing or stopping his swing prematurely, and probably that is its greatest virtue. But despite the virtues of the longbarreled gun for special purposes (and even these are open to argument) it is a pretty sad instrument for most shooting. On the duck flyway the gunner sees his bird coming a long way off. He has time to make a mental calculation as to lead, to track his target, pass it with the gun swinging, and fire. The trapshooter knows where his bird is coming from. He has his gun mounted at his shoulder, his cheek on the comb. He has only to swing up with his target, get ahead of it, and shoot with the gun swinging. On the other hand, the upland gunner usually doesn’t know exactly where his bird is coming from. He has to get on it fast and shoot fast. When a cock pheasant comes thrashing out of the brush behind him and heads for the trees, he has to get on it—now. He must be able to make a lightning-fast change of direction when a quail starts to curve around the tree or when a cottontail zigzags from one brush pile to another. For work of this sort the long-barreled gun is sluggish, unwieldy, and much too slow. Outdoor Life I grew up with such cannons. One of my first shotguns was a Winchester Model 97 pump with a 32-in. full-choke barrel. I was a rifle nut and I shot this ponderous old blunderbuss like a rifle. Give me plenty of time and something was liable to get hit. Doves flying innocently to roost or water, or ducks flying incautiously low, were my meat. But quail were something else. Where there was no brush and I could take my own sweet time, I wasn’t too bad. Complicate matters with some brush and trees, though, and I was sunk. I decided that for some mysterious reason I was just naturally attuned to doves and ducks, but that quail had my number. Then a great light dawned upon me. Presently I discovered a sucker who had a 20 gauge L.C. Smith that weighed about 6 pounds. He told me he couldn’t hit anything with it because 20 gauge guns aren’t powerful enough—that it didn’t shoot hard because the barrels were too short. What he was looking for, he said, was a good old 12 gauge with a 30-in. fullchoke barrel. Trying to keep my eager voice from trembling, I asked him if he would swap for my 12 gauge pump and give me 10 bucks to boot. He would. I grabbed the 20 gauge and the sawbuck and ran. ( He couldn’t hit anything with the 12 gauge either. He simply could not shoot, but I didn’t tell him that.) I’ve found it exceedingly important, in any upland hunting I’ve ever done, to have a fairly light gun. It’s also important that it be rather short of barrel, for a light, short gun handles fast. I know of nothing that weighs more than an extra pound—or even half a pound— in a shotgun. I have a fine pair of Winchester Model 21 doubles—a 12 gauge and a 16. Each has 26-in. barrels and stocks are exactly the same. The 12 weighs 7.2 lb.; the 16, 7 lb. The 16 seems much lighter than the 12. I often ask visitors to heft the two guns and estimate the difference in weight. Guesses run from 1 to 3 lb. The duck hunter can sit in his blind and wait for the ducks to come into the decoys. Trap and skeet shooters have only to lug their guns from the clubhouse to the firing line. The upland gunner, though, must carry his shotgun many miles in the course of a hunt. When I hunted desert quail in Arizona, I’d walk from 10 to 20 miles during the day. A grouse shooter from New England tells me he probably walks 3 miles for every shot he gets at a ruffed grouse. In Idaho and Washington I have on occasion shot the limit of three cock pheasants after walking only a few hundred yards, but far more often I’ve climbed and walked for miles. The heavier the gun, the wearier the hunter. For upland hunting that requires a lot of hiking a gun weighing 7.2 lb. is about as much as anyone should carry. One of 7 lb. is better, and he who latches onto a 6-lb. gun is lucky —if the gun throws enough shot and if he’s used to it. The short-barreled gun is livelier, faster-handling, and quicker-pointing than the long-barreled one. To me a double with 26-in. barrels is exactly right. The weight is between the hands and the gun comes up fast. For upland hunting even a pair of 28-in. barrels on a double seems a bit sluggish. I do most of my skeet shooting with a Remington Model 11-48 automatic with ventilated rib and a 26-in. barrel. It swings smoothly and beautifully, and I can break two or three more targets out of each 100 (or so I tell myself) than I can with any double. But the skeet shot knows when his bird is coming out, where it is going. Before he shoots, his feet are in position. And before he calls for the target, he does about 75 percent of the job of mounting his gun. The overall length of my 11-48 is just under 46 inches, while the overall length of my doubles is 43. For upland shooting, that fine Remington has just 3 in. too much barrel on it. For most field shooting I can do about as well with it as I can with a double, but on the tough snapshots—when a quail is zipping behind a bush or a big rooster is about to get over a ridge— I’m a little behind with it. With the shorter, handier double I’d have my bird centered. The difference lies, of course, in the receiver of the automatic, something which the double does not have. Stick a barrel of even moderate length on the end of a long receiver and your gun is overlong. For another Remington automatic, a little 20 gauge, I have two barrels—one 26 in. long and bored for skeet, the other 28 in. and bored modified. I’m going to have a variable-choke device put on the modified barrel to give an overall length of 23 in. Then I’ll really have an upland gun. A short barrel often has a good deal of muzzle blast. The hunter next to it in a duck blind wouldn’t love the man shooting it, and at traps the shooters to the right and left would cry out bitterly. But that is no skin off the nose of the upland gunner, who does not shoot cheek by jowl with anyone else. How should the upland gun be bored? That depends. The man who hunts grouse in heavy timber or bobwhite quail in the brush or follows the elusive cottontail—that man needs as wide a pattern as he can get. Skeet boring, which will usually cover from 28 to 32 in. at 25 yd., is about right for fast, short-range shooting. It’s also good for anyone with enough self-control not to shoot at over 30 yd. or so. It is no good at all for the man who shoots at everything that gets up, because beyond 30 yd. a lot of birds will get away wounded, even though they’ve been fairly centered. Read Next: Best Over/Under Shotguns Outdoor Life It is routine to recommend improved cylinder boring for upland game, but the term covers a multitude of patterns. To one manufacturer, an improved-cylinder barrel is one that patterns 35-40 percent. To another it’s one that patterns 50 percent. With the new shells with wadless crimps and gasproof overpowder wads, many guns marked improved cylinder pattern from 55 to 65 and sometimes 70 percent. As a rule, guns bored improved cylinder on the continent but used with the latest American ammunition won’t miss modified patterns by much. Read Next: Best Shotguns for Bird Hunting One American improved-cylinder gun patterns consistently from 50 to 55 percent; another covers as much area at 25 yd. as its maker’s Skeet No. 1 barrels. But at short ranges this particular improved cylinder throws a pattern with a denser center that carries out farther and gives clean kills at ranges where the Skeet No. 1 boring would only feather. The sloppy gun pointer in the uplands should use a wide-open bore and not shoot beyond its range. The sharp gun pointer can use more constriction and tighter, smaller patterns. Probably the ideal, all-round upland boring is one that gives 50 percent patterns at 40 yd. It’s easier to hit with such patterns at short ranges than with full-choke patterns, yet they’ll reach out and kill to 40 yd.—which is long range in the uplands. This 50 percent pattern is called quarter choke because in a 12 gauge it is often reached with a constriction of only 10 points (.010 in.), whereas in the old days 40 points’ constriction was considered necessary for full-choke performance. Very often this ideal 50 percent pattern is reached with barrels marked improved cylinder, sometimes with barrels marked modified. Actually, it is about the best all-round boring for the sporadic shooter, since most gunners do not have the skill to hit regularly at over 40 yd. anyway. For my part, I do more shooting with a double-gun bored modified and improved modified (60 and 68 percent) than with anything else. I like to reach out and knock down the occasional wild pheasant that runs ahead of a dog and gets up at 35 or 40 yd. Modified will nail them! Actually, though, 90 percent of all upland game is killed within 30 yd., and for that you want skeet or improved-cylinder boring. The 12 gauge gun tends to be a bit on the heavy side to be ideal for upland shooting, even if it’s a modern repeater with light alloy steel and dural receiver. My Remington Model 11-48 skeet gun weighs 7 3/4 lb., for example. A Remington Model 870 pump-action skeet gun in the rack weighs slightly less, 7 /12 lb., which is what my 12 gauge Winchester Model 21 double weighs. A Remington Model 11-48 skeet gun in 20 gauge with ventilated rib and 26-in. barrel weighs 7 lb. on the button. The 20 gauge, on the other hand, is a weapon only for the expert upland gunner, since it cannot be opened up quite as much as the larger gauges and requires sharper pointing. Bored quarter choke and improved modified, or even modified and full, it is a delightful and deadly weapon with 1 oz. of shot. I have a low-down, sneaking hunch that the queen of the upland guns is the 16 gauge, the gun that performs like a 12 and kicks and carries like a 20. About as near a thing to an ideal allround gun that I can imagine is a 7lb. 16 gauge bored quarter choke and modified—or, if a man is a pretty sharp pointer, even modified and full. Don’t let anyone tell you that a 16 bored modified is much behind a modified 12 in range; it isn’t. I have killed many pheasants at 45 yd. with a modified 16— and they didn’t move an inch when they hit the ground. I have killed plenty of ducks at 50-55 yd. with full-choke 16’s. The last two roosters I shot were a double. Four came boiling out of a brushy draw. I made a right and a left and the birds fell 43 and 48 yd. from the gun. The .410 and 28 gauges are like the 20, but more so; they simply cannot be opened up enough. I have shot a lot of grouse with a .410 and I have broken some pretty fair skeet scores with a 28, but neither is an ideal upland gun by any means. For my money the 16 is tops, the 20 next, and the 12 excellent if you don’t mind extra weight. Just as the upland gunner does not ne

https://theaviationist.com/2026/09/30/uk.text: A Ukrainian Air Force F-16AM takes off with full afterburner, carrying Sidewinder air-to-air missiles and drop tanks. (Image credit: Ukrainian Air Force) SHARE Belgium is set to deliver its first three F-16AM/BM fighters to Ukraine following a several-year delay, as Kyiv also discusses with Lockheed Martin about adopting the latest variant of the fighter jet. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy announced on Sept. 29, 2026, that Belgium will begin the transfer of its elderly F-16AM/BM Fighting Falcons to Ukraine by the end ‌of the year. The first delivery will see three aircraft sent, with the rest of the 30 promised aircraft being delivered as Belgium equips itself with F-35A Lightning IIs bought directly from the United States. The promised delivery follows a long delay, with the aircraft originally pledged in May 2024 to be delivered towards the end of the year and up until 2028. Unlike the Dutch and Norwegian F-16 deliveries, these transfers were held up by the slow roll out of Belgium’s F-35s, as the country was not willing to part with its combat aircraft until it had at least some replacements in service. To this date, only seven F-35s have been delivered to Belgium, of which three aircraft were delivered on Sept. 24 . Delivery of Belgium’s first four F-35s from the United States. They arrived in Belgium landing at Florennes Air Base in October 2025. (Image Credit: Belgian Ministry of Defence) Making the announcement, President Zelenskyy emphasised the importance of the deliveries of new kit to Ukraine to combat the Russian threat, with the expedited delivery of “F-16 ammunition from Belgium and other countries, including Spain” being instrumental to Ukraine’s air defence. These deliveries likely included a number of AIM-120 AMRAAM, AIM-9 Sidewinder air-to-air missiles and cannon rounds which are instrumental in the Ukrainian Air Force’s (UkrAF) defensive counter air campaign, shooting down large numbers of Russian drones and cruise missiles. The F-16s have also recently been augmented with the supply of the Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System (APKWS) guided rockets, which allow Ukrainian fighters to shoot down Russian drones at a far cheaper cost than the use of a normal missile. There is an important agreement with Belgium on the transfer of three F-16 fighter jets by the end of this year. We will work to receive these aircraft through an accelerated procedure. We have already received urgent deliveries of F-16 ammunition from Belgium and other… — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 29, 2026 On this point, during a meeting with Lockheed Martin representatives to discuss Ukraine’s future fighter capabilities, the Commander of the Ukrainian Air Force, Lieutenant General Anatolii Kryvonozhko, announced that F-16 pilots have shot down “over 3,150 enemy aerial targets which include 666 cruise missiles and an estimated 2,500 drones of various types.” The F-16 is a potent counter cruise missile and drone platform, having the speed to chase them down and destroy them before they impact civilian areas. The F-16 has also been an effective close air support platform, conducting “650 airstrikes” against the ground forces of the Russian Federation. The principle air-to-ground munitions employed by Ukrainian F-16s appear to be the GBU-39 Small Diameter Bombs (SDB). A single jet can carry up to eight of the 250 lb munitions without having to renounce to drop tanks and air-to-air munitions. Ukraine also employs several variants of the Joint Direct Attack Munition (JDAM). This weapon comes in a number of different weight classes, with 500 lb and 1000 lb variants seen in use in Ukraine, and can be equipped with a glide kit or a rocket kit to extend the range, however they have not yet been photographed on Ukrainian F-16s. ❗️Ukrainian F-16 pilots have shot down over 3,150 enemy aerial targets, including 666 cruise missiles and about 2,500 drones of various types, and have also carried out more than 650 airstrikes against enemy ground targets. This was reported by the Commander of the Ukrainian Air… pic.twitter.com/A9136JeJkF — 🪖MilitaryNewsUA🇺🇦 (@front_ukrainian) September 29, 2026 The F-16s and their Ukrainian pilots have proven themselves to be extremely effective since their introduction with the aircraft, now forming the bedrock of the current and future Ukrainian fighter force. However, the models delivered were all original A and B variant F-16s that were built in the 1970s and 1980s, making them similar in age to their former ex-Soviet fleet of aircraft. These fighters did receive a midlife update to extend their service lives and to give them more advanced air-to-air and air-to-ground capabilities. However, they are reaching the end of their useful service lives due to airframe fatigue and they are facing increasing maintenance demands after intensive use in the Russo-Ukrainian War. Belgian Air Component F-16AM fighter jet at RAF Waddington for Exercise COBRA WARRIOR in 2023. This fleet is transiting over to the F-35 as the air force modernises itself. (Image Credit: Crown copyright 2023/Sgt Nicholas Howe RAF) It was reported by the Wall Street Journal that maintenance of these aircraft is fast becoming an issue with an unnamed source stating that “more than half of Ukraine’s F-16s are currently in maintenance limbo” and that “Kyiv will exhaust the rest by the end of the year.” This is a worrying development if confirmed, as the F-16 is essential for Ukraine’s continued defence of its skies. Reportedly, this is due to delays at Sabena Aerospace Engineering, a Belgian company that is responsible for the long term maintenance of the F-16s used by Ukraine. Retired U.S. Navy Rear Adm. Mark Montgomery stated that the aircraft need to undergo regular phase inspections every 300 hours, which should take weeks. However, in Belgium it’s “taking as long as 40 weeks,” delaying maintenance and leaving aircraft unable to fly. More than half of Ukraine’s F-16 fighter jets are currently not operational due to maintenance delays in Belgium – WSJ A significant number of the fighter jets remain grounded due to a lack of spare parts and the need for more frequent repairs following intensive use. Given the… pic.twitter.com/9tWkGDSb8F — Jürgen Nauditt 🇩🇪🇺🇦 (@jurgen_nauditt) September 30, 2026 Details on this issue are scarce, but they paint a worrying picture for the UkrAF which has already undergone years of degradation due to the war. It is hoped that the integration of further aircraft into the force would alleviate some of these maintenance issues, allowing for a large pool of spare aircraft, and the possible maintenance of the jets in Ukraine itself. The importance of the F-16 to Ukraine’s current and future air force needs is likely what led to the meeting between Ukrainian representatives and Lockheed Martin to explore the possibility of supplying Ukraine with the far more advanced F-16 Block 70/72 , which uses capabilities derived from the F-22 and F-35 programmes. The introduction of newer jets could ease the maintenance burden as these aircraft would be fresh and infinitely more capable than their forefathers. Belgian Air Component F-16BM fighter jet at RAF Fairford for the Royal International Air Tattoo in 2024. This two seater was joined by F-16s from across the world to celebrate the 50th anniversary of the jet. (Image Credit: James Gray) Conor McGuire, Lockheed’s F-16 capability development lead, praised the work of Ukrainian pilots and ground crews and expressed his intention to help improve the aircraft Ukraine already operates. Whether this could be through further upgrades to the F-16AM/BM fleet or in the provision of further maintenance infrastructure is currently speculation. Ukraine’s Ex-Soviet Force Ukraine started the war with a mixed fleet of ex-Soviet aircraft which were already ageing out at the start of the conflict. Its mainstay air-to-air fighters in 2022 consisted of a force of around 70 MiG-29 Fulcrums and 34 Su-27 Flanker jet fighters, which bore a significant brunt of the early air war. When the Ukrainian ground based air defences had to be displaced during the opening days, it was up to these aircraft and their pilots to absorb the might of Russia’s air power. The MiG-29 and Su-27 fleets suffered several losses during those opening days, but they managed to stem the Russian tide long enough for the ground based air defences to secure the skies over Ukraine. Since then, these fleets have been upgraded to employ western missiles and bombs, including the AGM-88 High Speed Anti-Radiation Missile (HARM), which is used to suppress Russia’s air defence systems, as well as the 1,000 lb GBU-62 JDAM-ER and the 500 lb GBU-39B Small Diameter Bomb precision glide bombs. A MiG-29 of the 114th Tactical Aviation Brigade pulls a high speed manoeuvre. The leading edges of the wings and the horizontal stabilisers are painted in Ukrainian blue and yellow to ease identification during combat and prevent friendly fire at low level. (Image Credit: Ukrainian Air Force) Their primary role however remained air defence, with these aircraft maintaining the defensive counter air mission against missiles and drones until the introduction of the F-16. The actions of the 40th Tactical Aviation Brigade, who flew MiG-29s over Kyiv during the early days of the war, birthed the legend of the ‘ Ghost of Kyiv ’, the name of which was later awarded to them in 2024 via presidential decree. There have been a number of attrition replacements for Ukraine’s MiG-29 fleet, including 13 from Slovakia , 14 from Poland , along with a number of spare parts that allowed Ukraine to reactivate some of its stored fighters as well as three that Azerbaijan had in Ukraine for maintenance. However, losses have been heavy, with 39 aircraft visually confirmed damaged or destroyed, leaving the MiG-29 fleet significantly depleted over time. Colonel Oleksandr Oksanchenko’s Su-27 that he flew during the Royal International Air Tattoo in 2019. (Image Credit: James Gray) The Su-27 has not received any attrition replacements, with 20 confirmed lost over the course of the fighting. This included the tragic loss of Colonel Oleksandr Oksanchenko ‘ The Grey Wolf ’, Ukraine’s principal Su-27 display pilot, who was killed in combat on Feb. 25, 2022. His loss was sorely felt in the air show community, with the Royal International Air Tattoo dedicating a memorial to him at the show that same year. The memorial to the fallen pilot in 2022. His loss, amongst so many, was sorely felt. (Image Credit: James Gray) Ukraine’s primary air-to-ground aircraft at the war’s start were the 14 or so Su-24 Fencer and the 30 odd Su-25 Frogfoots which have also played key parts in the war to date. The Fencer fleet was essential early in the war to provide close air support and interdiction against Russian forces that landed at the Hostomel airport in 2022. Their attack here helped to block the runway that the Russian paratroopers of the VDV were going to use to bring in reinforcements by air, which gave the Ukrainian units of the National Guard the time to counter attack and contain the Russian landing. The actions here prevented the loss of Kyiv and allowed the country to stay in the fight for the long term. Ukrainian Air Force Su-24M Fencer with underwing Storm Shadow missiles from the front. (Image Credit: Vladyslav Demyanenko/Ukrainian Air Force) The Su-24 was also the aircraft chosen to carry the British, French and Italian donated Storm Shadow and SCALP-EG air launched cruise missiles (ALCMs), which have proven devastating against Russian supply depots, bridges and naval forces. Parts from the Panavia Tornado were bolted on to the airframe to allow for the missile to be integrated, allowing it to carry the weapon into combat. Due to this mission set, losses have been lighter than during the early war, as the Storm Shadow has a long stand-off launch distance, enabling the Su-24 to stay out of Russia’s air defences. However, the fleet has still lost 22 airframes in total, along with many of their pilots. Keen eyed observers will see that losses for the Su-24 are higher than their initial fleet total. This is thanks to the maintainers and engineers who were able to bring back a significant number of aircraft from storage, giving them a new lease of life to fight the invasion. ❗️Rare footage of the release of 🇫🇷French guided aerial bombs AASM Hammer from the board of a 🇺🇦Ukrainian Su-25 attack aircraft. pic.twitter.com/J7lFfzA0dr — 🪖MilitaryNewsUA🇺🇦 (@front_ukrainian) April 11, 2026 Likewise, the Su-25 has been Ukraine’s primary close air support weapon, delivering volleys of unguided rockets at long distance early in the war due to heavy losses . The supply of Soviet munitions dwindled over time due to a lack of resupply, and so the Su-25 took more of a backseat to the MiG-29 in the ground attack role. However, the fleet was significantly augmented with deliveries of French AASM Hammer bombs which gave the Frogfoot the stand off distance it needed to get back into the fight. Losses have still been unfortunately high, with 22 aircraft lost over the almost five years of war, significantly degrading the fleet. The ex-Soviet force of fighter planes and their pilots have soldiered on far longer than anyone had expected them to when the war started in 2022. However, it is the assistance of NATO and Ukraine’s Western allies that will enable the UkrAF to develop into the future. The Future Fighter Fleet The first F-16s entered Ukrainian airspace in August 2024, following extensive training programs abroad in multiple European partner nations as well as the United States. Jointly,they set up the European F-16 Training Center (EFTC) at the 86th Air Base in Fetești, Romania, which serves to train Ukrainian and Romanian pilots on the platform. Three Ukrainian F-16s flying in formation together, each is equipped for an air-to-air engagement, carrying AIM-120 AMRAAMs and AIM-9 Sidewinders, likely for counter drone missions. (Image Credit: Ukrainian Air Force) With this and several other training programmes in place, F-16AM/BM aircraft were then donated by Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands, and soon to be Belgium, to sustain the UkrAF. According to retired USAF pilot Lt. Gen. David Deptula , Ukraine’s F-16s now fly “80 percent” of all Ukrainian combat sorties, marking a significant change in the makeup of the overall fighter force. Even with the maintenance problems already discussed above, the F-16, being a Western jet, has more available spares than the ex-Soviet fleet, with the majority of spare parts being controlled by the Russian Federation. Ukraine currently has an estimated 39 F-16s in service, so far having lost five to attrition over the last few years, but it is expected to raise to a maximum of 80 aircraft once deliveries from Denmark and Belgium are completed. At that point, the F-16 will be the most numerous fighter in Ukrainian service. Cockpit photo from a Ukrainian Air Force F-16 Sept. 10, 2026, while defending against a Russian mass air attack. Off the aircraft’s starboard side, a Russian jet-powered Geran one-way attack drone can be seen falling from the sky, trailing smoke, having been shot down by the Ukrainian pilot—his third gun kill of the sortie, using the F-16’s 20mm cannon. (Image Credit: Official Ukrainian Air Force) Tragically, Ukrainian MiG-29 pilot Captain Andrii Pilshchykov ‘Juice’, who played a key role in advocating for the delivery of F-16s to Ukraine, was killed in a training exercise in August 2023. Following his initial wartime service, he spent months giving interviews to Western media and even traveled to the U.S. to meet and convince American lawmakers to enable the donation of the fighters to Ukraine. He was very much the public face of the campaign to see Ukrainian pilots in F-16s and their current impact on the war is in no small part due to his efforts. A message from ‘Juice’ — the Ukrainian MiG-29 pilot
